I have trained a few decision models (Kev 0.8B, 4B and 9B), and the results seem promising.

We have a training dataset (ISSP 2015 to ISSP 2024) of 14,356 participants with 616 general likert/choice questions about religion, politics, health, etc. (767,484 unique responses),
and a test set (SubPOP) with 133 US General Social Survey questions across 22 single-attribute personas (e.g., gender, political party). 

I trained three decision models on the training set to minimize the KL divergence, which measures the distance between two distributions: 

1. Kev 0.8B, which is based on Qwen 3.5 0.8B
2. Kev 4B, which is based on Qwen 3.5 4B
3. Kev 9B, which is based on Qwen 3.5 9B

Figure below shows sample questions from the test set (SubPOP dataset) on the political party subsample (democrat vs. republican). 
We compare baseline models (e.g., Kev 0.8) and trained models (e.g., Kev 0.8 FT) against the human sample (ground truth).
The model has not seen these questions nor the human sample distributions during training. 


![The distribution of responses from the human subpopulation and decision models](figures/political_party_mixed_kde_by_sample_subpop.png)

The figure shows interesting patterns:

1. As expected, larger baseline models do a better job in predicting the response distributions of people based solely off of their political party.
2.  The small baseline model (Kev 0.8B) performs poorly out of the box (KL = 0.5433), but when trained (Kev 0.8B FT), it outperforms larger baseline models in predicting new human distributions (KL(`Kev 0.8B FT`) = 0.3254 vs. KL(`Kev 4B`)=0.5168).

I think we could position the paper this way:

1. Researchers use silicon sampling is used to predict human responses.
2. LLMs are the type of models currently used for silicon sampling.
3. LLMs output text and are ill-suited for silicon sampling (i.e., predicting probability distributions of human samples).
4. Decision models are a new family of models that predict probability distributions based on a prompt.
5. Architecturally, decision models are more suitable for silicon sampling because they output the probability distribution of the responses directly.
6. Because LLMs and decision models are trained for output accuracy (e.g., determining whether a piece of code is safe or unsafe), they are not trained to produce probability distributions resembling human samples.
7. By training decision models on human respondent data we show that, conditional on a persona (e.g., gender or political party), decision models can learn to approximate human samples better than the baseline models.
   
So far this reads like a NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks paper.
To make it marketing, I'm taking one of the nutrition open datasets and predicting sample distributions on choice/likert questions using the baseline and trained Kev models.
I will compare the KL divergence of the human sample distribution (ground truth) against the model predicted distributions.
I'm expecting the trained decision models to considerably reduce the KL divergence compared to the baseline decision models. 
This would be genuine generalizability because the trained model is not trained on nutrition profiles or warning labels. 

To make the contribution stronger, as a post-hoc study, I thought what would happen if the researchers for the nutrition paper used our trained model to replace human respondents. 
I asked whether our decision model could replicate the regression results of the paper. 
This would give marketing researchers a glimpse into the end-to-end silicon sampling and how reliable it is for replacing human respondents.
I'm planning to run this next.
